title: National Parks
description: Can you find these iconic US National Parks on the map?

rounds.clue: The world's first national park, established in 1872, it sits atop a supervolcano and is home to more geysers than anywhere else on Earth.
El Capitan's sheer granite face draws the world's best rock climbers, while its valley floor is carpeted with wildflowers each spring.
Over five million years of erosion carved this mile-deep gash in the Colorado Plateau — one of the most recognizable landscapes on the planet.
The most visited park in the US, straddling the Tennessee–North Carolina border with misty ridgelines that give it its famous name.
rounds.answer: Great Smoky Mountains National Park, TN/NC

rounds.clue: America's largest subtropical wilderness, this watery park at the tip of Florida is home to manatees, panthers, and ghost orchids.
Towering sandstone arches — over 2,000 of them — dot this Utah park's landscape, including the iconic Delicate Arch.
Bryce Canyon's hoodoos — spire-shaped rock columns — glow orange at sunrise in this Utah park famous for stargazing.
Narrow slot canyons, massive mesas, and the Virgin River Narrows define this Utah park whose name comes from the Hebrew word for sanctuary.
This Colorado park contains the largest collection of late Jurassic dinosaur fossils in the world, including full Brachiosaurus skeletons.
The deepest lake in the US formed inside the caldera of a collapsed volcano. Its water is so clear you can see 140 feet deep.
Located on the border of Montana and Canada, this park's retreating glaciers inspired its nickname: the Crown of the Continent.
The highest peak in North America stands in this Alaska park — at 20,310 feet, it creates its own weather systems.
Olympic Peninsula's temperate rainforest receives up to 14 feet of rainfall per year, creating a lush moss-draped landscape in Washington State.
Active lava flows have been adding new land to this Hawaiian island park for centuries — you can watch molten rock enter the ocean here.
Joshua trees — found nowhere else at this scale — stretch across the meeting point of the Mojave and Colorado Deserts in California.
Below sea level in one of North America's hottest deserts, this California park holds the record for the highest air temperature ever recorded on Earth: 134°F.
Giant sequoia trees — the world's largest living organisms by volume — fill this California park's groves, some over 3,000 years old.
Rocky Mountain's Trail Ridge Road is the highest continuous paved road in the US, crossing the Continental Divide in Colorado.
White gypsum dunes stretching 275 square miles across New Mexico — the largest of their kind in the world.
Otherworldly clay spires and buttes in South Dakota, eroded by wind and rain, were once the hunting grounds of the Lakota Sioux.
Wind Cave in South Dakota contains the world's densest concentration of boxwork — a rare cave formation covering its walls like honeycomb.
Canyonlands in Utah is divided into three distinct districts by the Colorado and Green Rivers meeting at a Y-shaped confluence.
Mesa Verde's cliff dwellings were built by the Ancestral Puebloans over 700 years ago and abandoned suddenly around 1300 AD.
Carlsbad Caverns in New Mexico features the largest natural underground chamber in North America, and at dusk, a million bats spiral out into the sky.
This Texas park in the Chihuahuan Desert has peaks rising 8,000 feet above the surrounding plain, sheltering bears, mountain lions, and elk.
Shenandoah's Skyline Drive runs 105 miles along the Blue Ridge Mountains in Virginia, with stunning fall foliage views every October.
Acadia in Maine was the first national park east of the Mississippi River, with carriage roads donated by John D. Rockefeller Jr.
Biscayne in Florida is 95% water — protecting the third largest coral reef system in the world, just south of Miami.
Congaree in South Carolina protects old-growth bottomland hardwood forest — the largest intact expanse of it left in North America.
Mammoth Cave in Kentucky is the world's longest known cave system — over 400 mapped miles — still being explored today.
Indiana Dunes along Lake Michigan's southern shore features some of the world's fastest-moving sand dunes and an incredible diversity of plant species.
Voyageurs in northern Minnesota is a water-based park accessible only by boat in summer — it's named for the French Canadian fur traders who paddled these lakes.
Isle Royale in Lake Superior is the least visited national park in the lower 48 — a roadless island accessible only by ferry or seaplane.
Cuyahoga Valley in Ohio protects a stretch of the Cuyahoga River — the river that famously caught fire in 1969, sparking the Clean Water Act.
New River Gorge in West Virginia was the last national park established in the contiguous US (2020), protecting the world's oldest river.
rounds.answer: New River Gorge National Park, WV

rounds.clue: Capitol Reef in Utah preserves the Waterpocket Fold — a 100-mile long wrinkle in the Earth's crust — plus orchards planted by Mormon pioneers.
Great Basin in Nevada contains one of the world's oldest living organisms — a bristlecone pine over 4,900 years old — and a permanent glacier.
Channel Islands off the California coast are sometimes called the 'Galapagos of North America' for their unique wildlife found nowhere else.
Lassen Volcanic in California is the only place in the world where all four types of volcanoes are found within a single national park.
North Cascades in Washington contains more glaciers than any other area in the contiguous US — over 300 of them.
Kenai Fjords in Alaska is named for the glacially carved coastal inlets where tidewater glaciers calve icebergs directly into the sea.
Wrangell-St. Elias is the largest national park in the US — larger than the entire country of Switzerland — with nine of the sixteen highest peaks in the US.
Gates of the Arctic in Alaska lies entirely above the Arctic Circle and has no roads, trails, or facilities — the wildest park in the US.
rounds.answer: Gates of the Arctic National Park, AK

rounds.clue: Haleakala in Hawaii features a volcanic crater large enough to hold the entire island of Manhattan, and is the best place in the world to watch a sunrise above the clouds.
Guadalupe Mountains in Texas contains the world's most extensive Permian fossil reef and the highest peak in Texas.
Hot Springs in Arkansas protects thermal springs that have been used for healing since Native American tribes declared this land neutral ground thousands of years ago.
Petrified Forest in Arizona contains the world's largest and most colorful concentration of petrified wood — 225-million-year-old logs turned to crystal.
Saguaro in Arizona protects the iconic cactus that can live 150 years, grow 40 feet tall, and weigh up to 4,800 pounds when full of water.
Virgin Islands National Park covers over half of St. John island in the Caribbean, with coral reefs, sea turtles, and ruins of 18th-century sugar plantations.
Pinnacles in California protects the remnants of an ancient volcano that has been slowly moving northward along the San Andreas Fault for 23 million years.
Dry Tortugas in Florida is accessible only by boat or seaplane and protects the remote 19th-century Fort Jefferson — the largest masonry fort in the Western Hemisphere.
Theodore Roosevelt in North Dakota is where a young TR came to grieve and found the rugged Badlands landscape that inspired his lifelong conservation ethic.
Black Canyon of the Gunnison in Colorado has walls so steep and narrow that some sections receive only 33 minutes of sunlight per day.
rounds.answer: Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park, CO

rounds.clue: Great Sand Dunes in Colorado contains the tallest sand dunes in North America, formed by winds funneling through the Sangre de Cristo Mountains.
rounds.answer: Great Sand Dunes National Park, CO

rounds.clue: Redwood in Northern California protects the world's tallest trees — the coastal redwoods that can top 380 feet and live over 2,000 years.
rounds.answer: Redwood National and State Parks, CA
